nameStory: The Common Tan Wave gets its name from the soft, sandy tan coloring that washes across its wings like gentle waves on a beach. The 'wave' part also refers to the wavy lines that ripple across the wing surface, creating a subtle but distinctive pattern that catches the eye.
description: The Common Tan Wave is a small, delicate moth with wings that span just over half an inch across - about the size of your thumbnail. Its wings display soft tan and brown hues with subtle wavy lines running across them, giving it an understated elegance. As a member of the geometer moth family, it has a slender body and broad wings that it holds horizontally when at rest. This widespread little moth can be found throughout eastern North America, making it one of our more common nocturnal visitors.

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Look for delicate wavy lines crossing tan-colored wings, creating a subtle rippled appearance like sand patterns on a beach

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small wingspan of about 14-21mm - roughly the width of a dime to a nickel

idTips.label: Wing position
idTips.description: Rests with wings held flat and horizontal like most geometer moths, rather than folded tent-like over the body

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Warm tan to light brown overall coloring with subtle darker markings that blend softly together

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Slender, proportionally thin body compared to the relatively broad wings

habitat: You'll find Common Tan Waves in a variety of habitats since their caterpillars feed on such a wide range of plants - from woodland edges with oaks and chestnuts to gardens with goldenrod and bedstraw. They're often attracted to porch lights and outdoor lighting in residential areas, especially near diverse plantings. Look for them anywhere from sea level to moderate elevations where their host plants grow abundantly.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, typically May into June in New England. Look for them at outdoor lights on warm evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season - adults are most commonly seen from June through August. They're active at night and frequently come to artificial lights.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue flying well into fall, often until October. Late-season individuals may appear more worn with faded wing patterns.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - the species overwinters in an earlier life stage, likely as pupae in leaf litter or soil.

funFact: This tiny moth is one of nature's greatest travelers - it has managed to spread from North America all the way to the Galápagos Islands, nearly 1,000 miles off the coast of Ecuador, likely hitching rides on ships or flying incredible distances over open ocean!
confusionNotes: Several other small tan geometer moths look similar, but the Common Tan Wave's gentle, evenly-spaced wavy lines are more regular and pronounced than most. Remember: if the waves on the wings look like they were drawn with a steady hand rather than scribbled randomly, you're probably looking at a Common Tan Wave.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's 'common,' don't take this moth for granted - its incredible geographic range from Canada to South America makes it one of the most successful moths in the Americas, adapting to an amazing variety of climates and habitats.
compareHints: The Common Tan Wave is the only species in its genus Pleuroprucha found in New England, making identification easier once you learn its look. Compared to other small geometer moths in our region, it's distinguished by its particularly neat, wave-like lines and warm tan coloration. Many similar geometers have more irregular markings or cooler gray tones rather than the warm sandy hues of this species.
